blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Someone opens a pull request against the lesson's workflow, and the test job passes. Which jobs run?

options.text: test, image and deploy, since each job runs once the jobs it needs have succeeded
options.says: image and deploy carry if: github.event_name == 'push'; the output shows both skipped for pull_request.

options.text: test and image; deploy then waits for a person to approve it in the production environment
options.says: image is skipped on a pull request too: the output shows {'test': 'runs', 'image': 'skipped', 'deploy': 'skipped'}.

options.text: test only; image and deploy fail, because the if on each of them does not hold
options.says: A job whose if is false is skipped, not failed.

options.text: test only; image is skipped by its if, and deploy is skipped as well
options.says: Right: image's if is false, and deploy is skipped by its own if and because a job it needs was skipped.

origin.section: A Workflow Is Jobs, a Job Is Steps, and needs Orders the Jobs

questions.stem: In the lesson's workflow, where do the image and deploy jobs get their AWS credentials from?

options.text: An access key stored as a repository secret, which configure-aws-credentials reads
options.says: The workflow references no secrets (the program printed 'secrets referenced: []'); stored keys are the old way.

options.text: The test job, which assumes the role once and hands its credentials to later jobs
options.says: The test job has no role and no credentials at all; each AWS job assumes its own role.

options.text: A short-lived GitHub token, traded for a role's temporary credentials (id-token: write)
options.says: Right: OIDC; id-token: write lets the job request the token, and configure-aws-credentials trades it for the role's credentials.

options.text: moto's fake credentials, which the workflow sets so that no real account can be reached
options.says: moto is for the test job; image and deploy must act in AWS, through a role.

origin.section: CI Gets AWS Access From OIDC, Never From Stored Keys

questions.stem: Why does the lesson's workflow write each action's version as a 40-character hex string, with the release name only in a comment?

options.text: Because a commit SHA lets the action's owner move the job onto their newer releases
options.says: The page: a full-length commit SHA cannot move; it is a tag that its owner can move.

options.text: Because a seven-character commit prefix is what GitHub's hardening guide asks for
options.says: The guide recommends a full-length commit SHA.

options.text: Because a pinned action gets no access to the job's GITHUB_TOKEN or its permissions
options.says: An action is someone else's code running with your job's permissions, pinned or not.

options.text: Because a release tag can be moved by its owner, while a commit SHA cannot move
options.says: Right: a moved tag can make the next run execute different code; a commit SHA cannot move.

origin.section: Pin Every Action to a Commit and Give the Token Least Privilege
